title: The 30-Day IELTS Study Plan
subtitle: A calm, practical month of study for working learners aiming to move up from Band 5-6
description: A day-by-day and week-by-week plan that takes you from a baseline test to mock tests and test day. It offers flexible study-hour suggestions for busy learners and does not promise any score.
audience: Band 5-6 learners, including working professionals, who have about 30 days before an Academic IELTS test.

chapters.title: Start Here: Diagnose Your Starting Level
chapters.summary: Learn how this 30-day plan works and spend two days finding out where you really stand.
chapters.body:
This plan is for learners who are around Band 5 to 6 today and want to move up in one month. Thirty days is short. Some learners will gain half a band, some will gain more, and some will stay where they are. Nobody can promise a score. What this plan can give you is structure: every day has a job, and every week has a goal.

## How the plan is built

The month has four main weeks and a short finish. Week 1 builds foundations. Week 2 drills each skill. Week 3 adds the clock. Week 4 uses full mock tests and careful review. The last two days are for rest and light checks.

The study hours in this book are suggestions, not rules. A person who works eight hours in Motijheel and spends another hour in traffic has a very different day from a full-time student. Choose the version you can repeat every day, not the version that sounds impressive. Here are three sample patterns:

- Busy weeks: about 1.5 hours on weekdays and 3 hours on weekends.
- Steady weeks: about 2 hours on weekdays and 4 hours on weekends.
- Free weeks: about 3 hours on weekdays and 5 hours on weekends.

If load-shedding or office overtime ruins a day, do not try to make up everything. Do a short 30-minute session and continue tomorrow.

## Day 1: Listening and Reading baseline

Do not start studying blindly. Use the first two days to find your baseline. On Day 1, take one full Listening test and one full Reading test from a practice book you trust. Listening is about 30 minutes with 40 questions. Reading is 60 minutes with 40 questions, and there is no extra time to copy answers, so write your answers directly on the answer sheet as you go.

Use test conditions. No pausing the audio, no dictionary, no phone. Play the recording once only.

## Day 2: Writing and Speaking baseline

On Day 2, write one Task 1 report of at least 150 words and one Task 2 essay of at least 250 words. Give yourself 60 minutes in total. Remember that Task 2 counts double, so it deserves more of your time.

Then record yourself on your phone. Answer a set of Part 1 questions, one Part 2 cue card, and a few Part 3 questions. For Part 2, take 1 minute to prepare and then speak for up to 2 minutes. A full Speaking test lasts 11 to 14 minutes, so try to speak for a similar length.

## Record what you find

Make a simple table in your notebook with four rows: Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking. For each skill, write your raw score or honest feeling, and your three biggest problems.

For Listening and Reading, count correct answers and also note which question types lost marks, such as matching headings or map labelling. For Writing, check the four equally weighted criteria: Task Achievement or Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. For Speaking, listen to your recording and mark where you stop, where you repeat the same word, and where you could not finish an idea.

Example: Rafi works at a bank. He scored 24 out of 40 in Reading. He lost most marks on True/False/Not Given and ran out of time in the last passage. So his plan puts True/False/Not Given and timing first.

Tip: Be honest with yourself. A low baseline is not a failure. It is information, and it tells you where the next 28 days should go.
takeaways: Use Days 1 and 2 for a full baseline under test conditions.
Pick a daily study pattern you can repeat, not an ideal one.
Record question types and criteria that lose marks, not only totals.
A weak baseline is useful information, not a verdict.
chapters.exercise: Complete your four-skill baseline and write a table with one row per skill and your three biggest problems in each. Circle the single weakest skill.

chapters.title: Set a Realistic Target Band
chapters.summary: Turn your baseline and your real needs into a target you can work toward in 30 days.
chapters.body:
A target band is not a wish. It is a decision based on three things: what you need, where you are now, and how much time you have. Many learners skip this step and choose the highest number they can imagine. Then they feel disappointed in week three. A realistic target keeps you calm and focused.

## Start with what you actually need

Find out the exact requirement. A university, a visa office, or an employer will usually ask for an overall band and sometimes a minimum score in each skill. Check this on their official website or ask their admissions office directly. Do not rely on a friend, a Facebook group, or an old rumour, because requirements change.

Write down two numbers:

- Your overall requirement.
- Your minimum for each skill, if there is one.

The overall band is the average of your four skill scores, rounded by the official rules. This is why one weak skill can hold everything back. A strong Reading score will not fully hide a weak Writing score.

## Look at the distance

Now compare your baseline with your requirement. Use your honest notes from Chapter 1, not hope. If your baseline shows you at around Band 5.5 and you need Band 6.5, the gap is one full band. That is a large step for one month. It is possible for some learners, but it is not guaranteed. If the gap is half a band, the plan is more comfortable.

Progress is also uneven. Listening and Reading often improve faster once you learn question types and timing, because the answers are fixed. Writing and Speaking usually move more slowly, because they depend on language habits that take longer to change. Plan your expectations accordingly.

## Use three targets, not one

Instead of one target, set three levels:

- Minimum target: the score you must reach for your goal.
- Realistic target: the score you believe is reachable if you follow the plan.
- Stretch target: the score you would be happy to reach if everything goes well.

Example: Nusrat is a university student in Dhaka who needs Band 6.5 overall. Her baseline is close to 6.0. Her minimum target is 6.5, her realistic target is 6.0 to 6.5, and her stretch target is 7.0 in Reading. If her test is in 30 days, she also considers whether a later test date would be safer. That is a smart decision, not a weak one.

## Decide where to spend your hours

Your weakest skill gets the biggest share of time, but not all of it. Try this split as a starting suggestion:

- 40 percent on your weakest skill.
- 30 percent on your second weakest.
- 30 percent shared between the two stronger skills to keep them steady.

## Keep a flexible mind about the test date

If your mock results in Week 4 are far from your minimum target, you may choose to move the test date if the rules allow it. Check the cost and the rules early so that the choice is calm, not a panic.

Tip: Write your three targets on a sticky note and place it where you study. Review it every Sunday. If your evidence changes, change the plan, not your mood.
takeaways: Find the official requirement before choosing a number.
The overall band is an average, so a weak skill matters.
Use a minimum, realistic, and stretch target.
Give your weakest skill the biggest share of study time.
chapters.exercise: Write your minimum, realistic, and stretch targets for the overall band. Then write the official source where you checked the requirement.

chapters.title: Week 1: Build Your Foundations
chapters.summary: Use Days 3 to 7 to build daily habits in vocabulary, grammar, listening, reading, writing, and speaking.
chapters.body:
Week 1 is not about speed. It is about habits and basic accuracy. If you build a small daily routine now, the next three weeks will feel much easier. Days 1 and 2 were your baseline, so this week covers Days 3 to 7.

## A simple daily routine

Each day, try to include five short blocks. They add up to a manageable session even for a working learner.

- Vocabulary: 15 minutes.
- Listening: 20 minutes.
- Reading: 20 minutes.
- Writing: 25 minutes.
- Speaking: 10 minutes.

That is about 90 minutes, which fits a busy week. On a steady or free week, you can extend each block or add a second session in the evening. Treat these hours as suggestions. A consistent 90 minutes is better than a heroic five hours followed by two days of nothing.

## Vocabulary that you can use

Do not memorise long lists of rare words. Choose topic words you might really use: education, health, transport, technology, work, environment, and city life. Learn each new word in a short phrase, not alone. For example, write "heavy traffic in Dhaka" instead of only "traffic". Each day, pick five words, use each in one sentence, and say two of those sentences aloud.

## Grammar: fix your top three errors

Look at your Day 2 writing. Find your three most common errors. Typical ones are articles (a, an, the), subject-verb agreement, and tenses. Spend 15 minutes each day on one error only. Write five correct sentences, then check them against a grammar book or a trusted teacher.

## Listening and reading habits

For Listening, use short audio clips and practise listening for specific information: numbers, names, dates, and places. Listen once, write what you hear, then read the transcript and mark what you missed. For Reading, practise two skills: skimming for the main idea and scanning for names, numbers, and keywords. Read one passage slowly, then underline the words that told you the answer.

## Writing and speaking habits

For Writing, do not write full essays yet. Practise single paragraphs. One day, write an introduction for a Task 2 question. Another day, write a clear overview for a Task 1 chart. For Speaking, record yourself for two minutes every day on a simple topic such as your daily routine or your favourite festival. Listen once and fix one thing only.

Example: Imran, who works in an IT office, kept a daily log. On Day 3 he wrote "Vocabulary 15, Listening 20, Reading 20, Writing 25, Speaking 10". On Day 5, load-shedding cut his session, so he did a quick 30 minutes of Listening and Speaking only. He continued the next day without guilt.

Tip: End each day by writing tomorrow's first task on a sticky note. This makes it easier to start.

## End-of-week check

On Day 7, do a short review. Count how many days you followed your routine, and choose one habit to improve next week.
takeaways: Build a small daily routine of about 90 minutes.
Learn vocabulary in short phrases and use it aloud.
Fix your top three grammar errors one at a time.
Practise single paragraphs before full essays.
chapters.exercise: Write your own daily routine with five blocks and the number of minutes for each. Then follow it for Days 3 to 7 and count how many days you completed.

chapters.title: Week 2: Drill Each Skill
chapters.summary: Use Days 8 to 14 to practise question types and task types one at a time, and keep an error log.
chapters.body:
In Week 2, you stop practising everything at once and start drilling. A drill is a short, focused practice on one question type or one task type. The goal is not to finish many tests. The goal is to understand why you lose marks and to fix it.

## A weekly structure to try

For a working learner, a suggested structure for Days 8 to 14 is about 10 to 12 hours across the week. Many learners spread this as roughly 1.5 to 2 hours on weekdays and 3 to 4 hours on weekends. Adjust it to your life.

- Days 8 and 9: Listening and Reading drills.
- Days 10 and 11: Writing Task 1 and Task 2 drills.
- Day 12: Speaking Parts 1, 2, and 3 drills.
- Day 13: Mixed review of weak areas.
- Day 14: Rest or a light session, plus a weekly check.

## Start an error log

Buy a cheap notebook. Every time you lose a mark, write four things: the question type, what you answered, the correct answer, and the reason. The reason matters most. Was it a spelling error? A missed keyword? A wrong assumption? After a few days, you will see the same reasons again and again. Those repeated reasons are your real study plan.

## Listening and Reading drills

Pick one question type per session. For Listening, you might practise form completion, multiple choice, or map labelling. For Reading, choose True/False/Not Given, matching headings, or sentence completion. Do ten questions without a timer first. Then check every answer and write the reason for each mistake.

For True/False/Not Given, remember a simple idea: True means the passage agrees, False means it disagrees, and Not Given means the passage does not say. Do not use your own knowledge. Use only the passage.

## Writing drills

For Task 1, practise three steps: describe the main trend, write an overview, and give key details with numbers. Aim for at least 150 words. For Task 2, practise a clear plan: introduction, two body paragraphs with one main idea each, and a conclusion. Aim for at least 250 words. Because Task 2 counts double, practise it more often than Task 1. Judge your own work using the four equally weighted criteria, and note which one is weakest.

## Speaking drills

Practise each part separately. In Part 1, answer in two or three sentences, not one word. In Part 2, use the one minute of preparation to write keywords only, not full sentences, and then speak for up to two minutes. In Part 3, give an opinion, a reason, and an example.

Example: For the cue card "Describe a festival you enjoy", Mina wrote four keywords: Eid, family, food, new clothes. She spoke for nearly two minutes by moving through those words in order.

Tip: Record your Part 2 answer and listen for silence longer than a few seconds. Then repeat the same topic once more and try to fill the gaps.

## Weekly check

On Day 14, count your error log. Which three reasons appear most? Write them at the top of next week's page.
takeaways: Drill one question type or task type at a time.
Keep an error log and write the reason for every mistake.
Practise Task 2 more often because it counts double.
Use keywords, not sentences, in Part 2 preparation time.
chapters.exercise: Choose one question type you often miss and do ten questions. Write the reason for each mistake in your error log.

chapters.title: Week 3: Add the Clock with Timed Practice
chapters.summary: Use Days 15 to 21 to practise under real time limits and learn to manage your minutes.
chapters.body:
By Week 3, you know your weak areas. Now you add the clock. Many learners understand the material but lose marks because time runs out. Timed practice teaches you to work at test speed without panic. This week covers Days 15 to 21.

## A weekly structure to try

A suggested structure is about 12 to 14 hours across the week, with longer sessions on weekends. If you work long hours, protect at least one 3-hour block on a weekend morning. Here is one possible pattern:

- Days 15 and 16: Reading timed sections.
- Day 17: Listening full section.
- Day 18: Writing timed tasks.
- Day 19: Speaking mock and review.
- Day 20: Weak-area repair using your error log.
- Day 21: Rest or a light review.

## Reading: protect your 60 minutes

Reading is 60 minutes for 40 questions, and there is no extra time to transfer answers. A common guide is to spend about 20 minutes on each of the three passages, but you should adjust based on difficulty. If one question is taking too long, mark it, guess if needed, and move on. Never leave a blank, because a wrong answer and a blank score the same.

Practise one passage in 20 minutes, then two passages in 40 minutes, then all three in 60 minutes. Increase the load step by step.

## Listening: stay with the recording

Listening is about 30 minutes for 40 questions. The audio is played once, so you cannot go back. Before each section, use the preparation time to read the questions and underline keywords. If you miss an answer, let it go immediately. A single lost question should not cost you the next three.

Tip: Practise in a noisy place sometimes. If your home in Dhaka is noisy, that is normal. Use headphones and learn to ignore small distractions.

## Writing: split your 60 minutes

Writing lasts 60 minutes in total for two tasks. A common suggestion is about 20 minutes for Task 1 and about 40 minutes for Task 2, because Task 2 counts double. Keep a few minutes at the end to check spelling, articles, and word counts. Remember the minimums: 150 words for Task 1 and 250 words for Task 2.

## Speaking: practise the real length

A full Speaking test takes 11 to 14 minutes in three parts. Once this week, do a full practice. Ask a friend to act as the examiner, or record yourself and play the questions from a list. Listen to the recording the next day, not immediately, so you can hear it more clearly.

Example: Sabbir did a timed Reading practice and found that he spent 32 minutes on Passage 1. He decided to skip any question that took more than about one and a half minutes and return later. On the next attempt, he finished with five minutes to check.

## Review after every timed session

Timed practice is only useful if you review it. After each session, write one sentence: "I lost most time on ___." Then plan one fix for tomorrow. Do not worry if your scores drop slightly at first. Timing usually feels harder before it feels natural.
takeaways: Add time pressure step by step, not all at once.
Never leave a Reading or Listening answer blank.
Split Writing time with more minutes for Task 2.
After each timed session, write what cost you time.
chapters.exercise: Do one Reading passage in exactly 20 minutes. Write one sentence about where you lost the most time and one fix for next time.

chapters.title: Week 4: Mock Tests and Careful Review
chapters.summary: Use Days 22 to 28 to take full mock tests, review them properly, and make final adjustments.
chapters.body:
Week 4 is about proof and polish. You take full mock tests, you review them with care, and you make small final fixes. This week covers Days 22 to 28. Do not try to learn many new things now. Your job is to use what you have built.

## A weekly structure to try

A suggested structure is about 12 to 14 hours across the week. Weekends carry the mock tests, and weekdays carry the review. If you are very busy, you can do the four skills on separate days instead of one long mock. Here is a possible pattern:

- Day 22: Full Listening and Reading mock.
- Day 23: Review of Day 22 mistakes.
- Day 24: Full Writing mock, both tasks in 60 minutes.
- Day 25: Speaking mock and review.
- Day 26: Second Listening and Reading mock, or a repair day.
- Day 27: Review and error log summary.
- Day 28: Light revision and rest.

## Make the mock feel real

Sit at a table. Switch off your phone. Use a clock. Do not pause. Use a printed answer sheet if you can. If you usually study in the evening but your test is in the morning, try one mock at that time of day. This helps your brain get used to the schedule.

## Review is where improvement happens

A mock without review is only a test. A mock with review is a lesson. After each mock, spend at least as long reviewing as you spent taking it. For every wrong answer, ask three questions:

- Did I misunderstand the question?
- Did I miss the information in the text or audio?
- Did I know the answer but make a spelling or format mistake?

Group your mistakes. If most mistakes are spelling, practise spelling. If most are timing, practise pacing. Fix the biggest group first.

## Be careful with band scores

Practice scores are useful, but they are only a guide. Different practice tests vary in difficulty, and you may not feel the same pressure as in the real test. For Writing and Speaking especially, your own judgement can be too kind or too harsh. If possible, ask an experienced teacher or use a feedback tool you trust, and compare results over time rather than reading too much into one score.

Example: Tania took two Reading mocks, two days apart. She scored 27 in the first and 30 in the second. She did not celebrate too much, because the second test had easier topics. Instead she checked her review notes and saw that her True/False/Not Given errors had dropped. That was the real sign of progress.

## Final adjustments

In the last two days of Week 4, choose only a few fixes. For Writing, make a short checklist: answer every part of the task, give clear paragraphs, use a range of vocabulary, and check grammar. For Speaking, prepare a few reusable ideas about common topics such as hometown, work, study, family, and technology. For Listening and Reading, review your error log one last time.

Tip: Stop adding new materials. Repeating a few good resources deeply is more useful than collecting ten new ones.

## Check your target again

At the end of Week 4, compare your mock results with the targets from Chapter 2. If you are close to your minimum, keep going. If you are far away, decide calmly whether your test date should change.
takeaways: Treat mock tests like the real test: no pauses, no phone.
Spend at least as much time reviewing as testing.
Group mistakes and fix the biggest group first.
Use practice scores as a guide, not a guarantee.
chapters.exercise: After your next mock, sort every wrong answer into three groups: misunderstood, missed, or careless. Write which group is largest.

chapters.title: Test Day, the Final 48 Hours, and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Prepare your body, documents, and mind in the last two days, and plan what to revise next.
chapters.body:
The last two days are not for panic. They are for keeping what you already have. If your test is on Day 31, the final 48 hours are Days 29 and 30. This chapter gives you a calm checklist and a revision plan for the weeks after.

## 48 hours before: light and steady

On the first of the two days, study for about one to two hours only. Review your error log. Read your Writing checklist. Record a short Speaking answer to warm up your voice. Do not take a full mock. A bad result now may only damage your confidence.

On the second day, study even less, or take a break from study. Prepare your documents and your route. Many learners in Dhaka lose energy because of traffic and uncertainty, so decide how you will travel and leave extra time.

## Your checklist

- Check your booking details: date, time, and location.
- Prepare the identification document you used when you registered. Check the test centre rules to confirm what is accepted.
- Charge your phone and keep it ready, but follow centre rules about devices.
- Pack water and a light snack if allowed, and a pencil and pen as required by your centre.
- Check whether your Speaking test is on the same day or a different day, since this can vary.

## Sleep, food, and mind

Go to bed at a normal time the night before. Do not stay awake until 3 a.m. to study. Eat a normal meal. Avoid trying new foods. In the morning, do not read new materials. If you feel nervous, breathe slowly for one minute. Nervousness is normal and shows that you care.

## During the test

Listening: read ahead, listen carefully, and write short answers clearly. Reading: manage your 60 minutes and never leave blanks. Writing: plan for two or three minutes before each task, and keep the 150 and 250 word minimums in mind. Speaking: listen to the question, answer directly, and give a reason or example. If you make a mistake, correct it calmly and continue.

Tip: If you lose one answer, do not carry that worry into the next. Each question is a new chance.

## After the test

Do not review every answer in your head. Rest. Wait for your result. If the result is lower than you hoped, you have a ready system: baseline, error log, and weekly routine.

## Your revision plan

Whatever the result, keep a short revision loop. Here is a simple plan for the next four weeks:

- Week 1: Review your error log and rewrite your five most common mistakes.
- Week 2: Repeat drills on your two weakest question types.
- Week 3: Take one timed mock per skill, then review.
- Week 4: Take one full mock, compare it with your target, and decide what to do next.

Example: Farhana finished her test on a Saturday. She did not study on Sunday. On Monday she wrote down what felt easy and what felt hard. If she had to retake, she already had a plan.

Remember, this plan is a suggestion. You know your life best. Adjust it, but keep the habits: baseline, drills, timing, mocks, review, and rest.
takeaways: Keep the last 48 hours light: review, rest, and prepare documents.
Check your booking, ID, and travel plan in advance.
Sleep normally and avoid new materials on test morning.
After the test, keep a simple four-week revision loop.
chapters.exercise: Write your own final 48-hour checklist with at least six items, including documents, travel, sleep, and one light study task.
